newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy metalmen to strike, dispute may widen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy metalmen to strike, dispute may widen.

text.p: Italy's 1.5 million engineering and metalworkers will launch fresh strikes to press their pay claim in a dispute which may widen to embrace other industrial sectors, union officials said on Thursday.

Unions in the vital metal industry, which is the powerhouse of the Italian economy, called an eight-hour national stoppage for November 15 and also instructed regional branches to arrange four-hour walkouts in the intervening period.

Italy's three main national unions, the CGIL, CISL and UIL, said they would meet on October 17 to discuss ways to support the metalworkers in their dispute, which has become a battle over how to interpret a landmark 1993 labour pact.
"Employers want to keep salaries from increasing under the rate of inflation, repudiating the (1993) deal," Gianni Italia, leader of the FIM metalworkers union, told a news conference.
"This is a problem which concerns all of industry and because of this the October 17 meeting will decide whether to extend the strike to other sectors," he added.

The centre-left government said it hoped the conflict could be resolved swiftly and urged the two sides to resume stalled negotiations. Employers shrugged off the threat of escalating industrial action.
"As far as the strike is concerned, we've had lots of those over the last 50 years," said Innocenzo Cipolletta, the director general of employers' organisation Confindustria.
Talks between unions and management over the new metal workers' contracts broke down last month and no fresh contacts between the two sides are planned.
Unions have asked for a 262,000 lire ($172) pay rise per month for the 1997-98 period, part of which would be back payment for higher-than-expected inflation in 1995 and 1996.

The metal industry employers' federation Federmeccanica has rejected this demand, saying it would increase the cost of labour by an average 20 percent between 1996 and 1998 against target inflation for the same period of just 8.4 percent.
They have offered workers 180,000 lire a month.
At the heart of the dispute lies a labour deal signed in July 1993 by unions, employers and the government.
Under the terms of the pact, automatic index-linking of salaries was abolished, but management undertook to make up any shortfall in wages if inflation runs above government targets.

However the wording of the accord was deliberately vague. Unions have interpreted it to mean that all the inflation overshoot should be covered, employers argue that only a part of lost earnings need be made up.
The Fiom, Fim and Uilm metalworkers' unions on Thursday called on Prime Minister Romano Prodi to provide its own definition of the 1993 accord.
The government includes the ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) and is supported by the hard-left Communist Refoundation, and might be expected to back the unions.
But it has been reluctant to intervene in the argument, fearful that generous wage deals might ignite inflation.

"The wage accord has guaranteed a progressive and significant reduction in inflationary tension in our country. The common struggle against inflation must...continue over the coming months," Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said in a statement on Thursday. $ = 1,524 lire
